newsitem.title: FRANCE: Thomson-CSF seen worth many billions - paper.
newsitem.headline: Thomson-CSF seen worth many billions - paper.

text.p: If the French government decided to split up Thomson SA and sell Thomson-CSF and Thomson Multimedia (TMM) separately, the defence electronics stake could be worth 19 to 24 billion francs.
The La Tribune Desfosses newspaper on Monday quoted an unnamed Thomson-CSF official as saying, "The acquisition of Thomson-CSF could involve 24 billion francs ($4.6 billion)".
It also quoted the association of Thomson-CSF employee shareholders as saying the company was worth 19 billion francs, including eight billion for the 42 percent listed on the Bourse.
French Prime Minister Alain Juppe on Monday reiterated earlier statements by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis that selling Thomson in parts was one option.
The government on Wednesday suspended the planned sale of Thomson SA for one franc to Lagardere Groupe after an 11 billion franc capital injection.
Lagardere planned to buy out Thomson-CSF minorities and merge the company with its won Matra Defense Espace unit in a defence giant.
Lagardere would sell consumer electronics group Thomson Multimedia, also for one franc, to Daewoo Electronics of South Korea.
The government halted the process because the independent Privatisation Commission had objections against the terms of the TMM sale.
The Tribune said that if Thomson-CSF would be sold seperately, Lagardere, Alcatel Alsthom, Dassault, Sagem, Compagnie des Signaux and the SFIM could be candidates for a French solution.
The Les Echos newspaper went even further and foresaw a French "Lockheed-Martin" after a merger of Thomson-CSF with Matra and Aerospatiale and Dassault.

The future of Thomson Multimedia remains problematic because it has most of Thomson SA's debts and is loss-making. The government could sell it at a loss to either Daewoo under revised terms or to another candidate.

Or the government could make a capital increase after obtaining permission by the European Commission, oversee a restructuring until 1998 when TMM is expected to make profits and sell it at a later stage.

Whatever the decision, the government's moves will be closely followed by Philips Electronics of the Netherlands. The company went as far as officially denying on Friday that it had lodged or was planning to lodge a complaint with the European Commission against the Thomson capital injection.
But with its own Sound and Vision division, a rival to TMM, in financial dire straits, the Dutch group would look bitterly at any state money aiding a competitor.
